title: Three Things to Avoid in Middle Age If You Want to Stave Off Dementia
gist: A short write-up of a Neurology Open Access study led by NYU Langone's Josef Coresh using Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) data: avoiding smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure in midlife delays dementia by more than a decade. The piece stresses that 42 percent of Americans are at risk of dementia after age 55 and that current Alzheimer's drugs only slow progression rather than cure.

insights.claim: No cure for dementia exists and the newest Alzheimer's medications on the market only promise to slow disease progression, not reverse it.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Caps the realistic ceiling on anti-amyloid drug franchises — pricing and reimbursement debates hinge on 'slowing,' not curing.
insights.quote: While there are some new medications for Alzheimer’s on the market, even those only promise to slow the disease’s progression.
insights.locator: There’s obviously no cure yet for dementia

insights.claim: With no cure available, midlife risk-factor avoidance is the highest-leverage intervention against dementia — an ounce of prevention is worth more than any current therapy.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Value in dementia shifts toward screening, blood-pressure and metabolic control, and smoking cessation rather than late-stage therapeutics.
insights.quote: an ounce of prevention is worth even more

insights.claim: A new study in Neurology Open Access identifies smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure as the three biggest modifiable dementia risk factors to avoid in midlife.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Puts anti-hypertensives, GLP-1/diabetes control, and cessation products in the dementia-prevention narrative — a much larger addressable population than Alzheimer's drugs.
insights.locator: a new study published in the journal Neurology

insights.claim: Averting smoking, diabetes, and hypertension in midlife preserves brain health for more than a decade, according to study author Josef Coresh of NYU Langone.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A quantified 10+ year delay is the number payers and public-health budgets will anchor on when funding midlife screening.
insights.quote: “Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,”

insights.claim: 42 percent of Americans are at risk for developing dementia at any time after age 55, per Coresh.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A near-half-of-population risk pool defines the ceiling for diagnostics, long-term care, and prevention services demand.
insights.quote: “Discovering new ways to delay dementia is crucial with 42 percent of Americans at risk for developing the condition at any time after age 55.”
insights.locator: Discovering new ways to delay dementia

insights.claim: The findings rest on the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study, a longitudinal cohort followed for decades beginning in 1986 to examine the link between vascular problems and dementia.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Forty-year cohort data is hard to dispute and hard to replicate — it gives this vascular-dementia thesis unusual staying power in guidelines.
insights.locator: An international team of researchers led by Coresh

insights.claim: Framing dementia as downstream of vascular disease implies cardiometabolic control, not neurology, is where dementia burden actually gets reduced.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Watch for dementia-delay claims migrating into cardiometabolic drug labels and marketing.
